$ grep -v '^// [RE]' examples/saxpy.tiny
// SAXPY: y = alpha * x + y, the classic first CUDA kernel.
// We launch 5 threads for 4 elements: the "if (i < n)" guard stops thread 4
// from writing past the end, exactly like real GPU code must.
func saxpy(float alpha, float x[], float y[], int n) {
    int i = tid;
    if (i < n) {
        y[i] = alpha * x[i] + y[i];
    }
}
---
$ miniptx examples/saxpy.tiny
// Generated by miniptx: a PTX-like virtual ISA (not real PTX)

.func saxpy(.f32 %f1, .f32 x[], .f32 y[], .s32 %r1)
{
    mov.s32     %r2, %tid.x;
    setp.lt.s32 %p1, %r2, %r1;
    @!%p1 bra   L_endif1;
    ld.f32      %f2, [x + %r2];
    mul.f32     %f1, %f1, %f2;
    ld.f32      %f2, [y + %r2];
    add.f32     %f1, %f1, %f2;
    st.f32      [y + %r2], %f1;
L_endif1:
    ret;
}
---
$ miniptx examples/saxpy.tiny --threads 5 --run saxpy 2.0 [1,2,3,4] [10,10,10,10] 4
x = [1, 2, 3, 4]
y = [12, 14, 16, 18]
